extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in scientific method and causal inference (philosophy of science / experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical methods and canons for discovering causal relations by observation and experiment: Method of Difference, Method of Agreement, their joint/indirect form, Method of Residues, and Method of Concomitant Variations, together with precautions and limitations for applying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two instances (one in which the phenomenon occurs and one in which it does not) that are identical except for the presence or absence of a single antecedent; if the phenomenon appears only when that antecedent is present, infer causation. Best applied in artificial experiments where a definite change is introduced into a well-known preceding state of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: two instances differing only by A (presence/absence) or, practically, a previous state B C and a produced state A B C differing solely by the introduced A. Examples: bringing an object into a room or plunging a bird into carbonic acid gas — experimenter can be 'fully assured' (after repetitions) that no intervening circumstance caused the effect except the introduced change. Caveats/anti-patterns: spontaneous natural occurrences seldom provide such precisely matched pairs; there is a remaining doubt that the effect may have been produced by the means of producing the change rather than by the change itself (this can often be tested by other experiments); when the agency producing the phenomenon is a combination of antecedents that cannot be separated, the Method of Difference may be impracticable without prior use of Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine any instances in which a phenomenon occurs; if all such instances share a circumstance A, then A is connected (as an invariable antecedent) with the phenomenon. This yields laws of phenomena (uniformities) and suggests possible causes to be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: does not require special paired instances and is usable when artificial experimentation is impossible; it often suggests which antecedent to test by the Method of Difference. Limitations: Agreement alone does not establish causation (it may leave the question undecided whether A is cause or effect); one cannot be sure that the shared circumstance is the only common antecedent; best used to suggest experiments or as a secondary resource when Difference is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: THIRD CANON (Indirect/Joint Method of Agreement and Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, the circumstance in which alone the two sets of instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: perform a double employment of the Method of Agreement — show that all positive instances agree in having A, and that all negative instances agree in lacking A. This converts Agreement-evidence into the positive and negative instances required by the Method of Difference. Limitations: it is not equivalent to the direct Method of Difference because we can rarely be sure that the sets of instances agree in nothing else; the indirect method extends Agreement but lacks some of Difference's cogency; the negative instance in this method is effectively constructed by independent Agreement proofs rather than a single observed negative case.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOURTH CANON (Method of Residues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subduct from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents, and the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: subtract the known effects (deduced from prior inductions) from a combined phenomenon to infer the effect of the overlooked antecedent. This is a modification of the Method of Difference: the 'negative' instance is deduced rather than directly observed. Requirements and cautions: previous inductions (identifying effects of some antecedents) must have been obtained reliably (ideally by Difference); one must be certain that the residual phenomenon corresponds only to the remaining antecedent(s); otherwise evidence is incomplete. The residue-method is fertile for discovering obscure agents but must, where possible, be corroborated by producing C artificially or deducing its agency from known laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIFTH CANON (Method of Concomitant Variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: apply when total exclusion of a cause is impossible but its variations can be observed (quantity or relations change). Examples: tides varying with the moon's position (infer moon's causal role), pendulum disturbance by nearby mountain (remove pendulum), heat producing expansion when varied in quantity. Precautions: concomitance does not by itself determine directionality (cause vs effect) — attempt to produce one variation by means of the other to decide direction; retain other antecedents unchanged while observing the series of variations (i.e., use Difference-like control); numerical/concomitant relations often require knowledge of absolute quantities to deduce whether an effect is wholly due to a cause; extrapolating observed numerical laws beyond observed limits is hazardous (small observed ranges can be consistent with different laws), and hidden/counteracting causes beyond observed limits may vitiate inference. When A varies in quantity and a varies proportionally, one may infer that a is wholly or partly due to A; if absolute quantities are known, stronger numerical conclusions (e.g., proportionality, limits) can be drawn. The method is especially valuable where Difference is impossible but can also refine results found by Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions and general requirements for causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Across all methods, to infer causation reliably one must control or account for other antecedents, use repetition, ensure the means of producing a change are not themselves the cause, and, where possible, produce the effect by means of the proposed cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps emphasized in the text: choose a previous state of things well known so unforeseen alterations are unlikely to pass unobserved; introduce changes rapidly to minimize intervening alterations; repeat experiments to gain assurance; when the means of producing a change might themselves cause the effect, design additional experiments to test that possibility; when absolute quantities are relevant (concomitant variations), ascertain them if possible before inferring strong numerical laws; be cautious about extrapolation beyond observed limits; when many antecedents co-exist and cannot be separated, use Agreement (or the joint method) to suggest or narrow candidates for experimental isolation.
